questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Ireland and Cork were my second priority after Edinburgh and Scotland. I chose Cork as my second priority because of a previous study trip to Dublin, where I had really good experiences with the country and its friendly population. Additionally, I wanted to go to an English-speaking country to enhance my language skills. Lastly, because I am fascinated by the Irish scenery, especially the coastlines.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a bit of both. I think their office for international students did a good job, but there are many things and documents to keep track of, so it can seem overwhelming at times. My advice is to stay organized and not stress too much. The most important thing to be on top of is accommodation.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had a question or two, which I got answered via email from the office for exchange students.

How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
There is a housing shortage in Ireland, especially in larger university cities. I was not aware of this before I went. However, this means that there is pressure on the university, which cannot guarantee accommodation. Fortunately, I was relatively early and found something on my own in June. I would recommend starting the search earlier, as you compete on an equal footing with all the Irish students. Unfortunately, the accommodations are quite expensive. I paid around 800 euros per month for my housing (Brookfield Village Student Accommodation), which was worn and old by Danish standards but decent by Irish standards. This was incredibly cheap compared to many other exchange students who paid over 1000 euros and up to 1400 euros per month (for brand new ones). Mine worked out great, though, 30 minutes walk from the city center and 10 minutes from the campus.

Otherwise, I would consider looking into Seven North Mall or Scholar Lee. Those are probably some of the better options. Alternatively, there are the larger and more expensive ones like Yugo House, Broga House, and Ashlin House, but honestly, it's too expensive for what you get, in my opinion. Unfortunately, that's the current situation for students in Ireland - there are some significant economic forces making money off students, and due to the housing shortage, they can push the prices up.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off-campus in Cork is fine, as long as it's within the city itself. Most student accommodations are within a 30-minute walk to the university, and there are buses available, although they can be unreliable.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's a massive problem in Ireland that it's so difficult for students to find accommodation. It requires significant political decisions to address it. My best advice to Danish exchange students is to complete all the paperwork for Erasmus and KU so that you can be approved for UCC early. This way, you can get on their list for housing offers. However, don't rely solely on that; be proactive and start contacting private student accommodations, preferably as early as May or June.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, it was a bit challenging, especially with timetables. But I managed in the end, although not all of my desired courses were available. I think I could only take 2 out of the 6 courses I had selected from KU. Therefore, have a lot of backup options and be patient; it will work out in the end!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was a bit challenging because you had to be approved by the departments to take certain courses. This process could take some time, to the point where the courses had already started before receiving a response. But it worked out - I barely remember it now.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Office for International Students offered help via email and phone.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Getting only 2 out of the 6 courses is a bit disappointing, but it sounds like you didn't choose Cork primarily for the courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have a lot of backups in mind. Due to timetables, it's a bit challenging.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UCC primarily use 5 ECTS points for their bachelor courses, meaning I had 6 courses simultaneously. It didn't work for me, and I find it academically challenging to achieve depth with only 2 hours of instruction per week. Consequently, I feel I had 6 very superficial courses compared to UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had 3 third-year courses, 2 second-year courses, and a language course for exchange students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As mentioned above, I find courses with 2 hours of instruction (lecture) to be insufficient, and it became too superficial for me.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Maybe this one (GV3216 Contemporary Ecological and Anti-Capitalist Politics) because of the lecturer. However, it was very specific and narrow. It was heavily linked to reading novels about utopias.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There were no unexpected expenses in my budget. However, expect the cost of living to be almost the same as in Denmark, maybe just 10% cheaper. So, it's an expensive place to be on exchange, as my expenses increased significantly during this period compared to in Denmark (I went out more for drinks, on more trips/excursions, ate out more, etc.).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing is expensive! Additionally, eating and drinking out are also almost the same as back home. Groceries might be slightly cheaper. Public transport is cheap (bus/train) with their Leap Card.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Infinite clubs and societies at the university for free. Additionally, free access to the university's large fitness center with gym, sports halls, a swimming pool with sauna, and an athletics facility. I joined UCC Soccer after a trial and also participated in hiking trips with UCC
Mountaineering.It
's a great way to meet Irish students and other exchange students as well.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything from rugby to step dancing on the sports front, and on the association front, everything from the Harry Potter Society to the Socialist Society. There was a lot, and it takes up a significant portion of the campus. I was pleasantly surprised by that.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: UCC Mountaineering is great for getting out and exploring Irish nature on full-day hikes every Sunday for around 10 euros. You get to visit some places that are challenging to reach without a car. UCC Soccer was fantastic for me as a football player, especially because it provided social interaction with some Irish guys.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: My advice is to go on weekend trips as much as possible - this is some of my best memories. And take advantage of the opportunity to rent a car. It just makes things easier! I would recommend Killarney, Kerry Peninsula, the Dingle Peninsula, and, in general, their national parks. Additionally, a trip to Dublin is a must.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it quite easy - it's not far from Denmark, and the Irish are sweet and friendly. Additionally, the pub culture was fantastic.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Clubs and Societies are probably the best way. Otherwise, hope to find a place where you have Irish roommates. People don't talk much in class. Otherwise, it's at the pubs.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Irish students start university early (18-19 years old), so they are quite young. This could be noticeable at times.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The pub culture and the Irish friendliness, hospitality, and sociability.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
About the city: Cork is small, not particularly picturesque, and not grandiose. However, I found it cozy, and I think it represents the authentic Ireland (more than Dublin). Additionally, UCC has a significant presence in the city, contributing to a good vibe. I never felt unsafe in the city.

About the Irish: They are sweet, talkative, and friendly. It's a bit harder to connect with young Irish people, but it's definitely possible.

About UCC: Cozy and beautiful campus, the academic level is below UCPH (University of Copenhagen) but still fine.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress about the exchange - everything will work out, even though the paperwork may seem overwhelming. Try to have a structured approach, and it will be fine. When you're there, go on as many trips and visit as many pubs as possible. That's where my best memories come from. Try to say yes to as much as possible and be proactive on your own.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting people from all over the world - and meeting the Irish. Additionally, the fantastic trips into the beautiful Irish nature and the enjoyable moments at the Irish pubs.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Experiencing more solitude than I'm used to - but it was also cool to try.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
